v.q: What does `@Cacheable` do on a method?
o: Returns the cached result for the same key and skips the method
Runs the method twice in a row for extra safety
Stores the result as a new row in a database table
Caches only the exceptions that the method throws
v.w: It is implemented by a proxy (cache-aside). On a miss it runs the method and stores the result under the key.

v.q: Which statement about @Cacheable is NOT true?
o: The method always runs
The result is stored under a key
A hit skips the method
The cache name must be configured
v.w: On a hit the method is not called, which is the whole point of the cache.

v.q: Which annotation removes stale data after an update?
o: `@CacheEvict`
`@Cacheable`
`@CacheConfig`
`@EnableCaching`
v.w: `@CachePut` updates the entry with the new value and always runs the method. `@CacheEvict` removes entries.

v.q: Which annotation updates the cache with the new result every time the method runs?
o: @CachePut
@CacheEvict
@Cacheable
@EnableCaching
v.w: CachePut always runs the method and stores the result. CacheEvict removes entries.

o: A hot entry expires and many requests hit the source at once
The cache runs out of disk space under heavy load
Two caches end up holding different copies of data
A cache key collides with another key of the same hash
v.w: Mitigate with `sync = true`, jittered TTLs, request coalescing or refresh-ahead.

v.q: Which @Cacheable setting helps against a cache stampede?
o: sync = true
A bigger heap
More threads
A shorter TTL
v.w: Spring offers sync = true on @Cacheable so only one caller loads the value.

v.q: Why should cached account balances usually have a short TTL, or not be cached at all?
o: A stale value can mislead users or drive wrong decisions
Caches are not able to store numeric values at all
Balances never change over the life of an account
TTLs are not supported for entries that hold numbers
v.w: Cache data that is read often, changes rarely and tolerates some staleness. Money values need strict freshness or event-based eviction.

v.q: Which data is a poor fit for a long-lived cache?
o: An account balance
A currency list
A country list
Product descriptions
v.w: A stale balance misleads users. Slowly changing reference data suits caching.

v.q: A cache lives in each JVM instance (Caffeine). What happens when one instance updates data?
o: Other instances keep stale copies until they expire or are evicted
All the instances update themselves instantly and together
The cache is shared between them automatically by Spring
The update fails with an exception on every other node
v.w: For shared state use a distributed cache such as Redis, or publish eviction events to all nodes.

v.q: Which cache choice keeps several instances in sync?
o: A shared Redis cache
Caffeine in each JVM
A static map
A ThreadLocal
v.w: A per-JVM cache gives each instance its own copy. A shared store gives one.

v.q: A `@Async` method is called from another method in the same class. What happens?
o: It runs synchronously, because the call bypasses the proxy
It runs on a new thread, exactly as the annotation suggests
Spring throws an exception when the application starts
It runs twice, once in each of two different threads
v.w: Like other proxy features, `@Async` works only when called through the bean from outside. Call it from another bean.

v.q: Which call runs a @Async method on another thread?
o: A call from a different bean
this.method() in the same class
A call from the same class constructor
A private method call
v.w: Only calls through the proxy are asynchronous.

v.q: Why configure a custom `TaskExecutor` for `@Async` instead of relying on defaults?
o: To bound the pool and queue, name threads and handle rejection
Because Spring does not create any default executor at all
To make the methods run in the caller's own thread
To remove the need for a proxy around the bean
v.w: Unbounded or misconfigured pools can exhaust memory or threads. Name threads for easier debugging.

v.q: Which statement about the default @Async executor in production is NOT true?
o: It is always the right size for production
An unbounded queue can fill memory
You can name its threads
You can bound its pool
v.w: Defaults may be unbounded, so configure the pool and queue yourself.

v.q: Where does an exception thrown in a `void` `@Async` method go?
o: To the `AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler`; the caller never sees it
Back to the caller, the same as with a normal call
It is retried automatically by Spring a few times
It stops the whole application from running
v.w: Return a `CompletableFuture` so the caller can handle failures, or register an uncaught exception handler that logs them.

v.q: How do you get the result or an exception from an @Async method?
o: Return a CompletableFuture
Return void
Print a log line
Use a static field
v.w: The Future carries the value or the exception to the caller. A void method sends errors to the handler.
